Title: Your Rollback Is Untested and You Will Find Out at 3am
Abstract: Most teams treat rollback as the safety net that makes everything else acceptable. Ship fast, we can always revert. I believed that too, until the night I tried to revert an automated deployment and found that the revert did not work either.  The change had been written by an agent. It touched more than I thought, in ways that were individually reasonable, and undoing it turned out to be a careful manual unwind rather than one command. That is a bad thing to learn while a service is down, and it is the specific reason I stopped accepting "we can always revert" as a reason to let anything automated ship something unbounded.  Since then I have treated the rollback path as something that has to be tested on purpose, the same way you would test anything else you depend on in an emergency. This talk is how I do that. How I bound a change so reverting it is genuinely one step. How I verify the revert actually runs instead of assuming it will. And what I found once I started deliberately breaking things to see whether recovery behaved the way I expected it to.  I will be honest about the cost, because this slows you down. The useful question is not whether to do it but which changes deserve it, and I will tell you where I draw that line and why.  For anyone whose pipeline has a revert path nobody has ever exercised in anger.

Title: A Rule Is a Door: What Changes When You Enforce an AI Agent's Rules in Code
Abstract: A coding agent that runs unattended for months is told what not to do in sentences. Does it listen? I kept each rule of one such agent in two forms: a sentence in an instruction file and, for some rules, code on the path of the action (a hook that refuses, a write path that rejects, a scheduler precondition). In a preregistered replay of 5 rules, 200 runs, one sentence cut violations from 100% to 0% on 2 rules and to 10% or 20% on 2 more. The door alone did not hold: 53% of runs still broke the 4 rules it covered, and one hook never fired in 10 of 10 runs that broke its rule. Where the write hook blocked, the block took effect 10 of 10 times. The talk covers the cases and what I check before I trust a guardrail.

Title: Life of a token: from agents to silicon and back
Abstract: What really happens between your agent's prompt and the GPU in a self-hosted AI stack?  Every AI agent call ends up as tokens on a GPU somewhere, and most developers never see what happens in between. In this talk we follow a single token from an agent running in Kubernetes, through an AI gateway that enforces identity and policy, through an inference-aware router, down to vLLM on bare-metal GPUs, and all the way back. Along the way you'll learn why LLM traffic breaks traditional load balancing, what prefill and decode mean for latency and cost, and what it takes to run the whole stack on infrastructure you control.

Title: From 173 Billion Documents to Training Data: A Beginner's Tour of LLM Data Processing
Abstract: A model learns everything it knows from its training data. Where does that data come from, and what makes text suitable? This talk answers both questions based on our work at Fraunhofer IAIS  The running example is OpenGPT-X, the project that produced the open Teuken models. I follow its data from a raw Common Crawl dump to a clean, deduplicated corpus: what curated sources and web crawls each give you, why metadata normalization matters, how filtering removes 96.94% of web documents (and why that is the pipeline doing its job), and why deduplication consumes 80% of the compute budget.  Every claim comes with an honest number, from CPU hours to euros per document. By the end you will know how a training corpus is built, and what that tells you about the models trained on it. No data-pipeline experience needed.

Title: Evals for Generators: Testing an LLM That Writes Clinical Configuration
Abstract: When an LLM writes prose, "looks good" might be enough. When it generates clinical configuration and test protocols, such as allergy skin-test setups and EHR note templates, a wrong answer becomes a patient-safety ticket. This talk covers how I built an evaluation harness for an AI-driven configuration and test-protocol generator. It includes golden datasets built from real (de-identified) configs, schema and rule-based validators that run before any LLM judge, diff-based regression tests across model and prompt changes, and SME review loops that turn expert corrections into new test cases. We'll look at which metrics predicted real-world defects and which ones were vanity numbers. The methods carry over to any structured-output generator, whether it produces SQL, YAML, JSON, or forms.  **Takeaways:** 1. Layer deterministic validators before LLM-as-judge. 2. Build golden sets and regression gates for structured outputs. 3. Close the loop with domain experts at low cost.

Title: Defending the AI Factory: Practical Security Strategies for MLOps
Abstract: As machine learning models transition from experimental notebooks into critical production systems, they become primary targets for sophisticated cyberattacks. Standard DevOps security is no longer enough to protect the unique components of the machine learning lifecycle.  This intermediate-level talk dives deep into SecMLOps (Security in Machine Learning Operations), exploring how vulnerabilities manifest across the entire ML pipeline. Attendees will learn how to secure data ingestion pipelines against data poisoning, protect model registries from unauthorized tampering, mitigate supply chain risks in Python dependencies, and defend deployed endpoints against adversarial and extraction attacks. Through real-world architectural patterns and practical toolchains, this session provides actionable strategies to build resilient, secure, and compliant AI systems without stalling developer velocity.

Title: Adding Tamper-Evident Audit Trails to AI Agents in Production
Abstract: AI agents are making real decisions in production - calling APIs, writing code, moving data. But most teams have no reliable way to prove what an agent did, when it did it, or whether the output was modified after the fact. When something goes wrong, you are left digging through logs that anyone could have edited.  This talk covers a practical approach to solving that problem: hash-chained, cryptographically signed audit trails that plug into the agent frameworks teams already use - CrewAI, LangChain, Haystack, LiteLLM, and others.  I will walk through how Asqav adds tamper-evident logging to agentic workflows with a few lines of code. Every agent action gets recorded in a hash chain (each entry references the previous one, so you cannot insert or delete entries without breaking the chain) and signed using ML-DSA-65, a post-quantum digital signature algorithm standardized by NIST. The result is an audit trail that is independently verifiable - anyone can check that the record has not been altered.  The talk will focus on real production concerns:  - Why standard logging and observability tools are not enough when you need to prove integrity, not just observe behavior - How hash-chaining and digital signatures work together to create tamper evidence without requiring a blockchain or external service - What it looks like in practice: adding audit trails to a CrewAI agent pipeline in under 10 lines of Python - How this maps to EU AI Act requirements around traceability and record-keeping (Article 12) - Performance overhead, storage considerations, and key management tradeoffs in production deployments - Multi-party approval workflows - requiring human sign-off before an agent executes sensitive actions  This is not a theoretical talk. It is based on a production-ready open-source toolkit (1,700+ tests, pip-installable) that teams are using today. The audience will leave with a clear understanding of how to add verifiable audit trails to their own agent systems and why this matters for compliance, debugging, and accountability.

Title: Research to Reliable ML: Lessons from a Deep Learning Pipeline for Skin Lesion Classification
Abstract: Building a machine learning model that performs well in an experiment is only one part of developing a reliable ML system. Reproducibility, data quality, evaluation methodology and deployment readiness are equally important, particularly in healthcare applications where model predictions could eventually inform clinical decisions.  In this talk, I will use my research on deep learning for skin lesion classification as a case study to explore the practical considerations involved in developing an end-to-end medical imaging workflow. My work combines U-Net segmentation with CNN architectures, including ResNet50, VGG16 and EfficientNetB4, and achieved a reported AUC of 0.99 on the evaluated PH² dataset.  I will discuss the challenges of structuring image-processing and classification workflows, maintaining consistency across preprocessing and evaluation, interpreting performance metrics, and recognising the limitations of results obtained from a single dataset. I will also examine what would be needed to move from an experimental research pipeline towards a more reproducible, monitored and deployment-ready ML system, including versioned data and models, automated testing, experiment tracking and independent validation.  Using this case study, I aim to demonstrate why reliable machine learning requires more than selecting an architecture and achieving a strong metric. It requires a systematic approach to the entire lifecycle, from data preparation and experimentation to validation, monitoring and maintenance.

Title: Agent Protocol Engineering: Designing Reliable Multi-Agent Systems
Abstract: Multi-agent systems promise powerful AI architectures, but coordinating autonomous agents is notoriously difficult. Without proper protocols, agents produce inconsistent outputs, fail silently, create race conditions, and become impossible to debug. This workshop teaches systematic approaches to building reliable agent-to-agent communication. You'll learn to design structured message protocols using Pydantic for type-safe agent interactions, implement validation layers that catch errors before they cascade, handle concurrent agent execution with proper synchronization, create observable agent workflows using OpenTelemetry, and build fault-tolerant systems that gracefully handle agent failures. Through practical exercises, you'll construct a distributed AI system where specialized agents collaborate on complex tasks: a research agent gathering information, an analysis agent processing data, a synthesis agent creating reports, and a validation agent ensuring quality. Each agent communicates through well-defined protocols with automatic retry logic, dead-letter queues, and comprehensive logging. You'll implement real-world patterns: event-driven architectures for agent coordination, circuit breakers for failing agents, semantic versioning for protocol changes, and testing strategies for non-deterministic systems. Walk away with production-ready patterns, debugging tools, and architectural blueprints for building multi-agent systems that actually work in production.

Title: You Can't Rerun Sunlight: Designing ML Data Architectures for Physical AI
Abstract: In software, when something goes wrong, we often retry. In machine learning, we rerun a pipeline, backfill missing data, or reproduce a model with the same code and inputs. But what happens when that model is connected to the physical world?  In physical AI systems, data comes from sensors, cameras, robots, and real environments. It can arrive late, be corrected later, or never be captured at all. After a backfill, yesterday’s dataset may look complete even though the model making a decision yesterday did not have that information.  This talk explores how to design ML data architectures that preserve not only what we know now, but what the system knew at the time a decision was made. I’ll share lessons from building data infrastructure for robotics and machine learning in agriculture, including late-arriving data, backfills, point-in-time reproducibility, and tracing data from physical events through ML pipelines and downstream decisions.  You can rerun the pipeline. You can rerun the model. But you can’t rerun sunlight.

Title: Running 50+ AI agents in production: the patterns that held up
Abstract: I build and run a platform of 50+ Claude agents on Amazon Bedrock at Ruby, a US AI startup. They research companies and the people in them, and write briefings before sales calls, for real customers every day.  Getting the first agent working was the easy part. This talk is about what comes next: keeping dozens of agents accurate, measurable and affordable once real traffic arrives.  What I'll cover, with real traces and numbers:  Let the AI suggest, let the code decide. Scores, formatting and anything that changes a customer's data stay in normal code. It's cheaper, and you can actually test it. Know when quality drops. Quick code checks on every run, and AI judges on a sample of about 1,500 runs a month. One lesson: a judge that can't see what the agent saw will mark correct answers as wrong. Giving it the tool results took one answer from 0.2 to 0.95. Keep the bill under control. We cut our cost per run by about 75%. A big part was prompt caching, which also breaks without any error: a date in the system prompt or tools in a different order is enough. I'll show how to catch it, including a limit I measured on live Bedrock. Make it fast. Running independent agents in parallel cut the time to research a company from about 32 minutes to 11. You'll leave with a short checklist you can use on your own agents the next day.

Title: Send Metadata, Not Video: Running Computer Vision on Existing CCTV with Poor Connectivity
Abstract: Small and mid-sized retailers already own many CCTV cameras, but streaming that video to the cloud for AI analysis is too expensive. In many markets, the internet connection simply can't carry it. This talk shares how we built a computer-vision analytics system for physical stores that runs people counting, age and gender estimation, queue monitoring and heatmaps on NVIDIA edge devices on site, and sends only anonymised metadata to the cloud.  I'll cover the pipeline architecture (DeepStream modules, ONNX conversion, and what runs at the edge versus in the cloud). I'll also explain how we built our own training data when public datasets didn't match the stores' environments, how we kept models updated across distributed devices, and the privacy benefit of never moving video off site, including the mistakes we made along the way.  **Key takeaways**  1. A reference edge/cloud split for multi-camera computer vision 2. Building and annotating a domain-specific dataset on a startup budget 3. Operating and updating models on a fleet of edge devices

JobTitle1: Senior Staff Software Engineer, Enterprise Architecture and AI
Title: Harness Engineering for Production LLMs: Eval-as-Code From Day One
Abstract: An evaluation harness is the difference between an LLM application you can change with confidence and one that becomes a write-only system. Traditional MLOps has model metrics and a validation set. LLM systems have prompts, retrieval, tool calls, and a model you do not control, and the CI pipeline has to cover all of it.  This talk shows how to build reusable evaluation harnesses with lm-evaluation-harness, RAGAS, DeepEval, and Promptfoo: eval-as-code in CI, behavioral regression suites, faithfulness scorecards, and the operational practices that keep eval coverage growing as the application grows. We cover dataset versioning alongside prompt and code versions, what to gate a deploy on versus what to alert on, and how to catch the silent quality drops that follow a provider-side model upgrade.  Takeaways: A reusable harness pattern that works across RAG and agentic systems. CI integration patterns for LLM evaluation. What belongs in a deploy gate. Operational practices for keeping evals current as the system evolves.  Audience: ML and MLOps engineers, AI engineers, QA engineers. Level: Intermediate.

Title: Running vLLM Inference on Kubernetes Across Clouds: A Production-Ready GPU Blueprint
Abstract: If you’ve tried vLLM locally, you’ve seen how fast it can generate tokens. The real challenges appear when serving production traffic: multiple models, 100s of concurrent requests, pod failures, and unpredictable tail latency. These are the same issues repeatedly raised by the community when running vLLM on Kubernetes.  In this talk, I’ll share an open-source, Terraform-driven vLLM production stack that runs consistently on EKS, AKS, GKE, and Nebius Mk8s. The talk is based on my upstream contributions to the official vLLM production stack. We’ll cover GPU-optimized Kubernetes deployments for vLLM workloads, tiered inference, and end-to-end automation, from cluster bootstrap to SSL-enabled, inference-ready endpoints, along with built-in observability using Grafana dashboards.  This session is aimed at platform engineers and MLOps teams building GPU-backed LLM inference w/o cloud lock-in.

Title: Stop AI Agents from Making Up Facts: Graph-RAG for Reliable Data Retrieval
Abstract: AI agents don't just answer wrong—they act wrong. When agents hallucinate during execution, they fabricate API parameters, invent confirmations, and make decisions based on false data. Traditional RAG retrieval makes this worse by returning approximate matches instead of precise answers.   In this hands-on session, we'll build a travel booking agent and compare two approaches: traditional vector search (FAISS) vs Graph-RAG (Neo4j knowledge graph) on 300 hotel FAQ documents.   You'll see how structured knowledge graphs eliminate fabricated statistics and incomplete retrieval—achieving better accuracy on precise queries. Walk away with a working pattern you can apply to any domain where AI agents need reliable, verifiable data retrieval. No prior graph database experience needed.

Title: Ledger to Lake: Automating Database DevOps for ML in Finance with BigQuery, Liquibase, and Harness CI
Abstract: In regulated financial institutions, deploying Machine Learning models is often bottlenecked not by algorithms, but by rigid database change management and audit requirements. Traditional MLOps pipelines frequently fail to address the critical "Data DevOps" gap, leading to schema drift, failed deployments, and compliance risks when model features depend on evolving database structures.  This "Tale from the Trenches" session details how we engineered a robust, zero-downtime deployment pipeline for our production ML systems using Google BigQuery, Liquibase, and Harness CI. We moved beyond theoretical MLOps to solve real-world friction: ensuring that every model deployment is intrinsically linked to a versioned, verified database schema change.  Attendees will learn:  The Architecture: How we integrated Liquibase to manage BigQuery schema versioning as code, treating database migrations with the same rigor as model artifacts. The Pipeline: How Harness CI orchestrates the handoff between database migrations and model deployment, implementing automated verification gates that prevent schema-model mismatches. The War Story: A candid look at a critical failure where a silent schema change threatened production model integrity, and how our new pipeline now catches these errors before they reach production.  The Result: How we reduced deployment cycles from weeks to hours while achieving 100% audit compliance for database changes in a highly regulated environment.  This talk is for MLOps engineers, Data Platform leads, and DevOps practitioners struggling to bridge the gap between database operations and machine learning lifecycles in enterprise environments. Leave with actionable patterns for implementing Database DevOps in your own ML pipelines.

Title: Your Agent Failed Mid-Run. Logs Won't Replay It.
Abstract: In production, a multi-step agent can fail mid-run: a bad tool call, a wrong intermediate answer, a broken handoff. Logs usually confirm that something broke. They rarely give you the run back so you can inspect the exact step and try another path. The usual next move is to re-run everything: more time, more tokens, and the same live side effects again.  This talk is about a practical habit for that failure mode: record → replay → fork. Save the full agent run as a local cassette (e.g. prompts, tool calls, and results). Replay the same steps to find where it went wrong. Fork from that step with a fix, and check it before you re-run in production.  Demo: a failed multi-step agent run. We rewind to the bad step, fork a fix, and show recovery without re-running the whole pipeline. Traces help you observe; a cassette lets you reproduce the run and change one decision. Flashback is one way to keep those cassettes. The talk teaches the habit, not a product pitch.  You leave with: how to treat a failed agent run like a replayable artifact next to logs, traces, and re-runs.

Title: Coding Noisy Product Names for Consumer Price Statistics: Trie Rules, Bag-of-Words and Reliability-Weighted Labeling
Abstract: We ran a 1D-CNN, an LSTM and a character n-gram logistic regression head to head on the same noisy-product-name task, under one matched training protocol. The logistic regression won every category. This talk is about why, and about what that means for anyone classifying short, messy text.  The setting is consumer price measurement from alternative data: scanner exports, web-scraped listings, transaction and receipt records. They promise broader coverage, and they arrive as short, abbreviated, inconsistently spelled product names with no standard product code. Before any price can be compared, every item has to be mapped to a consumption classification such as COICOP. The method has separately been deployed in production on data that cannot be released; everything measured in this talk comes from the public benchmark.  I will go through the pipeline step by step: domain-specific normalization and tokenization of noisy item names, a prefix-tree (trie) pre-classifier driven by per-category key phrases and stop phrases, and a per-category binary confirmation model that decides whether an item really belongs to the category the rules assigned. I will explain why binary confirmation per category beats one multiclass model here, and what that choice costs you.  One operational lesson worth the ticket on its own: rules look like they are solving the problem, and then they are not. They cover only 32 to 50 percent of items, and coverage erodes as new product names appear. The learned stage is permanent infrastructure, not a stopgap you remove once the rule set matures.  Labels are the other half. The protocol has several annotators giving a binary valid/reject judgment, with votes aggregated by a reliability weight that updates as annotation proceeds. The model sits inside the same rule, so fine-tuning is continual rather than a periodic project. Around 66 labeled examples per category turn out to be enough.  Then the numbers: mean F1 0.997 for the character n-gram logistic regression, word-order features adding nothing, the neural baselines behind. The benchmark is synthetic and public, and I will say plainly what that does and does not establish.  Takeaways: where the bottleneck in noisy short-text classification actually sits, how to structure annotation so it compounds instead of decaying, and how to recognize the case where reaching for a larger, order-sensitive model is the wrong move.  Method, benchmark and reproducibility package: arXiv:2606.02004

Title: Running an AI agent fleet behind a write-gate: what broke and what we changed
Abstract: Foreman+ is an open-source fleet of three AI agents (Google ADK, Gemini on Vertex AI, Cloud SQL Postgres with pgvector) that turns a technician's nameplate photo and voice notes into a field-service job record. Every fact passes a write-gate before the fleet can remember it: cheap deterministic checks first, then an LLM verifier. If the verifier errors or returns nothing, the write is refused.  This talk is the build log. A setup prompt that named a job by street address instead of ID made an agent write a technician's name onto a different job at the same address. The gate refused it as a contradiction, but the real fix was in the prompt. On the camera glasses, switching photo compression to medium cut capture time from 34 s to 6.3 s. A camera frame sent before the question was ignored and the model answered from imagination; attached inside the question turn, it was right 3 times out of 3 in our probe. I'll also cover what the repo admits it still lacks: every service runs at a single instance, and there's no CI yet.  In the recorded demo run the fleet made 14 proposals in 83 seconds and the gate refused one. The repo is MIT-licensed and the demo runs without a login.

Title: From Prototype to Millions of Daily Renders: Shipping LLM-Powered Features Reliably at E-commerce Scale
Abstract: Getting an LLM-powered feature to work in a demo is easy. Serving it on a high-traffic e-commerce page millions of times a day, without hurting latency or showing customers a bad answer, is a different job.  Drawing on shipping AI shopping features at Amazon that reached millions of daily page renders with zero faults, this talk covers the operational side of putting generative AI on a critical page:  - Deciding when content should be generated in real time and when it can be precomputed - Latency budgets, timeouts and fallbacks so the page never waits on a model - Quality gates and monitoring that catch bad output before customers see it - Integrating with an existing AI assistant's orchestration without becoming its bottleneck - Launching safely: gradual dial-ups, kill switches and the metrics that matter  Attendees leave with a practical checklist for taking an LLM feature from prototype to production traffic.

Title: Self-Signed Evidence: Why Your LLM Agent's Green Checks Prove Nothing
Abstract: An LLM support agent finds two orders for the same blender, picks one and calls the refund tool. Code confirms the order is the customer's, recent and under the limit, then pays. The broken blender was in the other order.  Putting the check in code did not help: it trusted an order ID the model chose. I call this self-signed evidence.  I build LLM agents that spend customers' money. In public τ²-bench runs I counted 82 of 1,632 conversations where tools accepted a change to an order the task never asked to change; in at least 21, the model picked the order itself.  You will learn to find the model-written values your checks trust, test a check with a swapped order ID, and run it in shadow before it is allowed to block. For engineers whose agents issue refunds or make bookings.

Title: Your Agent Works. Will It Survive Tomorrow? Operating LangGraph.js with skein-js
Abstract: Your agent reviews a support ticket, proposes an action, and pauses for approval. The reviewer returns tomorrow. Meanwhile, your server has restarted, you’ve deployed a new version, and the submitting system has retried its request. The approval must still exist, the retry must resolve to the original work, and an operator needs to understand what happened. Building a useful agent is only the beginning of running a dependable service.  This talk introduces skein-js, an open-source, self-hosted TypeScript server runtime for LangGraph.js agents. LangGraph provides graph execution, checkpointing, and interrupts. skein-js supplies the infrastructure around those graphs: persistent API resources, background execution, streaming, and an operator console, while retaining existing LangGraph.js graphs and SDK clients.  Through an issue-triage demonstration, we’ll follow a workflow through duplicate submission, human approval, and a server restart. We’ll examine how Postgres persistence and Redis-backed background work support reliable execution, where idempotency guarantees end, and how telemetry helps explain failures. Attendees will leave with a concrete architecture for operating agents on infrastructure they control and failure scenarios they can use to evaluate any agent runtime.

JobTitle1: Senior AI Systems & Web Engineer | Technical Lead
Title: No Dataset, No Benchmark: MLOps for Lebanese Sign Language
Abstract: There was no Lebanese Sign Language dataset to download, so we built one: 40,000+ samples collected with Deaf community members, volunteers and NGOs. This talk is about the unglamorous MLOps underneath: rejecting bad landmark extractions before they reach training, models that are allowed to say "I don't know", and reading a 98% internal result without fooling yourself.

Title: From Pilot to Production: Rolling Out AI Coding Agents Across a Regulated Enterprise
Abstract: Moving AI coding agents from pilot to production inside regulated enterprises — evaluation frameworks, governance and compliance guardrails, developer adoption tactics, and lessons on what actually scales.

Title: The Fairness Paradox: Why Your Compliant ML Model May Be Causing the Most Harm
Abstract: AI fairness regulations are tightening globally — but passing a disparate impact audit may not be enough. This talk introduces the Dollar-Cost Fairness Framework, developed through FairLens: an open-source credit-decisioning analysis tool built on 95,588 real HMDA mortgage applications.  We trained and evaluated 10 machine learning models — from logistic regression to neural networks — measuring not just accuracy, but the dollar-denominated harm imposed on protected groups. The findings are striking: a Support Vector Machine and a Neural Network achieved near-identical AUC scores, yet the SVM imposed $227M more in disparate harm against Black and Hispanic applicants. That is a 13x difference in financial harm between two "equally accurate" models.  We will walk through: - Why accuracy metrics systematically obscure fairness gaps in high-stakes lending - How Dollar-Cost Fairness translates model bias into regulatory and business risk ($) - AIF360 bias intervention techniques (reweighing, calibrated equalized odds) and their real tradeoffs - A live demo of FairLens showing model comparison, fairness dashboards, and bootstrap-validated results (p < 0.001)  Attendees will leave with a reusable evaluation framework, concrete code patterns for integrating fairness audits into ML pipelines, and a clearer picture of what "AI agent risk" means when agents are making financial decisions about people's lives.  This talk is for ML engineers, data scientists, and AI practitioners building or auditing decision systems — especially in regulated domains like finance, insurance, or hiring.

Title: Securing the AI Stack: From Models to Agents to Infrastructure
Abstract: Training the model is the easy part. Shipping an AI system you'd trust with real data, real tools, and real actions is where teams stall, usually because nobody has a map of where the risks actually live.  In this lightning talk, I'll give you that map: a four-layer defense-in-depth framework for production AI, with the one threat and one fix that matter most at each layer.  Model: indirect prompt injection. Fix: validate every output before it drives an action. Agents: over-permissioned agents. Fix: tool allowlists and approval gates for irreversible actions. Tools and MCP: poisoned or unvetted tool servers. Fix: allowlist, schema-validate, and pin them like dependencies. Infrastructure: poisoned weights and silent exfiltration. Fix: scan models in CI/CD and restrict egress.  Every layer has holes, but stacked together they leave no straight path from attacker to impact.  You'll leave with a 16-question checklist, four per layer, that you can run against your own pipeline this sprint.

Title: Building Reliable LLM-Powered Autonomous Testing for Modern MLOps
Abstract: As software systems become more complex, engineering teams need testing approaches that can scale with rapid development cycles and evolving application architectures. Traditional automation frameworks based on hardcoded locators and deterministic scripts often require significant maintenance effort, making it difficult to support continuous delivery at enterprise scale.  This session presents Autonomous Cognitive Navigation (ACN), a Natural Language Based (NLB) generative framework designed to make software testing more adaptive, reliable, and easier to maintain. ACN applies Large Language Models to interpret application states, reason through workflows, and execute complex end-to-end testing scenarios using natural language instructions instead of fragile test scripts.  The talk explores the architecture and engineering decisions behind ACN, including its State-Aware Reasoning Loop, Persistent Temporal Action Memory, Semantic Canonicalization approach, and multimodal end-state verification capabilities. These components address common challenges in AI-driven automation, such as maintaining context across long workflows, reducing unnecessary processing of UI information, and validating outcomes despite application changes.  The session also shares practical results from applying this approach across thousands of localized application variants and more than 70 languages. ACN achieved a 95% reliability rate while reducing new test flow onboarding efforts from 120 hours of manual scripting to under 4 hours of natural language definition.  Attendees will learn how LLM-based automation can be designed, evaluated, and integrated into modern engineering workflows to improve testing reliability, reduce maintenance overhead, and support scalable software delivery. The session is intended for MLOps engineers, developers, QA practitioners, and technical leaders interested in applying AI capabilities to real-world software operations.

Title: Compliance as a Pipeline Stage: Automating AI Governance in MLOps
Abstract: Most ML teams treat compliance as a review that happens before launch. Under the EU AI Act, U.S. AI governance frameworks, and privacy laws, that approach breaks down, because models are retrained, redeployed, and updated continuously.  This talk shows how to move governance into the MLOps pipeline itself. Drawing on experience building automated GDPR compliance systems, ROPA reporting pipelines, and data governance platforms at Meta, Arpita covers:  Risk classification at model registration Lineage capture across datasets, features, and model versions Policy checks as CI/CD gates before training and deployment Monitoring signals that feed compliance evidence Documentation generated automatically from pipeline metadata  The talk also covers practical trade-offs, including where automated gates slow teams down and how to keep engineering and compliance aligned without manual handoffs.

Title: Shipping Agentic AI to Production: What a Regulated Enterprise Learned the Hard Way
Abstract: A practitioner talk on moving agentic AI from demos to production in a regulated enterprise: per-agent identity and least-privilege access, risk-adaptive policy gates that auto-approve low-risk actions and escalate high-risk ones, immutable audit, and evaluation as a platform-enforced MLOps gate — grounded in public agent benchmarks and production failure patterns, plus 20 years of platform work including a 20,000-pipeline migration. Takeaway: a reference pattern — identity, scoped grant, policy gate, audit — and a checklist for operating agents in production.

Title: AI Gardening for MLOps: Managing Context, Memory, and Entropy in Agentic Systems
Abstract: Most AI demos are short. Production MLOps and agentic AI workflows are not.  Long-running systems accumulate instructions, retrieved documents, tool outputs, partial plans, stale assumptions, and memory from prior work. None of that looks like a normal service failure, but it can still change behavior: the system keeps responding, tools keep working, and the workflow slowly becomes harder to reason about because its context has drifted.  This talk introduces AI Gardening as a practical discipline for building and operating agentic engineering systems. We will look at what teams need to design once an agent or LLM workflow moves beyond a single prompt: what context is allowed into a workflow, what should expire, what must be preserved for audit, when memory should be scoped or reset, how to detect contradictory instructions, and how to make working state inspectable during real engineering tasks.  The goal is not to make probabilistic systems pretend to be deterministic. It is to make the operational environment around them maintainable: bounded context windows, explicit memory ownership, reset boundaries, retrieval evaluation, artifact handoffs, and evidence that lets humans understand why the system behaved the way it did.  Attendees will leave with a checklist for more reliable AI workflows: treat context as production input, separate durable knowledge from temporary working state, make memory auditable, design reset paths before drift becomes a failure mode, and give humans a clear way to inspect state instead of trusting a transcript.

Title: From Agent Trace to Reproducible Regression Test
Abstract: A TypeScript agent can produce the expected answer while skipping a required lookup, repeating a side effect, or recovering through an invalid path. Output evaluation alone does not explain which behavior needs a regression test. This practical session follows a deliberately broken agent through a local trace-to-test workflow: inspect the execution tree, isolate the relevant events, express a narrow behavioral invariant, and rerun a keyless fixture in CI. Attendees will learn how to check required dependencies and retry boundaries without asserting one exact path for every valid run, and how to retain a redacted failure artifact another engineer can review. The walkthrough distinguishes recorded tool success from observed task outcome, and explains why missing telemetry remains unknown rather than proof that an action never happened. Examples use Vitest/Jest and the free, MIT-licensed AgentInspect project maintained by the speaker. The method complements existing evaluation and production-observability systems; it is not a replacement for runtime authorization or a product sales pitch.

Title: Who Is Calling Your Model? Identity and Authorization for AI Agents and ML Pipelines
Abstract: Your ML platform is full of non-human actors: training jobs pulling data, inference services calling feature stores, CI pipelines pushing models, and now AI agents calling tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) on behalf of real users. Most of them authenticate with shared API keys or over-privileged service accounts, and very few teams can answer: which workload made this call, on whose behalf, and how do I revoke it?  This talk walks through a practical identity architecture for ML and agent systems, based on lessons from building identity products for AI agents:  - Workload identity instead of secrets – giving pipelines, model servers and agents verifiable identities (SPIFFE/SPIRE-style) and short-lived credentials instead of long-lived keys. - Delegated access for agents – how an agent should get scoped, user-bound access to tools and APIs: OAuth token exchange, MCP authorization, and registering agent clients with Client ID Metadata Documents. - Guardrails in the loop – where human approval, step-up and revocation belong when agents take real actions. - What goes wrong – over-scoped tokens, confused-deputy calls between services, invisible agent-to-agent hops, and the missing kill switch, with fixes for each.  You'll leave with a reference architecture and a checklist you can apply to your own ML platform and agent deployments.

Title: Which Workload Owns This GPU Metric?
Abstract: GPU telemetry starts with a device identifier. An ML platform starts with a job, pod, model, or team. Those names do not line up.  This talk shows how we built an OpenTelemetry Collector processor that joins node-level GPU data to the Kubernetes workload using the device. We will follow one metric from its GPU UUID through device allocation, pod discovery, and workload ownership until it becomes useful for capacity, performance, and failure analysis.  The join is the interesting part. MIG changes what a device means. Pods move. Short jobs disappear before a cache refreshes. Device assignments and telemetry arrive on different clocks. A mapping layer can quietly attach the right metric to the wrong workload unless it preserves uncertainty.  We will build the attribution path, examine its Kubernetes API and RBAC boundary, and then break it with the cases above. The result is ordinary OTLP with pod, namespace, deployment, and job identity. No backend-specific GPU model is required.  This is a systems talk about the missing layer between GPU monitoring and useful MLOps telemetry.

Title: Operationalizing Agentic LLMs: Building and Evaluating DevMate at Scale
Abstract: Moving agentic LLM systems from experimentation into real developer workflows requires more than capable models. It requires scalable orchestration, continuous evaluation, observability, and reliable feedback loops. This session explores DevMate, a centralized agentic LLM platform designed to support developer workflows across complex Android Open Source Project codebases at Meta.  DevMate combines static code understanding with dynamic contextual signals to support agentic tasks including code transformation, debugging assistance, and architectural reasoning. The session examines the architecture behind these workflows and the engineering considerations involved in operating them consistently across diverse development scenarios.  A central focus is DevMate's evaluation infrastructure, which uses graders, benchmarking pipelines, and feedback loops to assess model outputs, compare performance across tasks, and align model behavior with developer expectations. By embedding evaluation and observability into the platform, teams can make improvements measurable and reproducible while maintaining quality standards.  Attendees will gain practical insights into designing agentic LLM platforms, building evaluation pipelines, monitoring model behavior, and balancing autonomy, reliability, and developer trust in production-oriented AI workflows.

Title: Building a Production-Ready Voice AI Agent with LangGraph, RAG and Evaluation
Abstract: Building an AI agent is easy. Making it fast, reliable, observable and useful in production is much harder.  In this talk, I’ll share lessons from building a voice-first AI tutoring system using LangGraph, RAG, OpenAI Realtime, FastAPI, PostgreSQL and pgvector.  I’ll walk through how the system combines retrieval, agent workflows, semantic caching, verification and conversational memory while keeping latency low enough for a real-time voice experience. I’ll also cover the operational challenges that appear once an AI prototype meets real users: retrieval quality, agent failures, evaluation, tracing, latency and cost.  We’ll look at how evaluation and observability can be built into the development lifecycle using retrieval metrics, agent traces and systematic testing rather than relying on whether an LLM response simply “looks good.”  The session will focus on practical engineering decisions, trade-offs and lessons learned from taking an Agentic AI system beyond the prototype stage and operating it as a real product.  Attendees will leave with a practical approach to designing, evaluating and operating RAG and agent-based applications in production.

Title: From Agents to Systems: Orchestration, Recovery, and Economics
Abstract: Agentic AI shows strong promise in BFSI, but production deployments surface challenges that go far beyond model performance. This talk shares real-world lessons from deploying multi-agent systems in regulated environments, focusing on three critical areas: reliable orchestration across legacy systems, recovery through verification and repair agents, and the economics of autonomous execution. It explains why separating planning, execution, authorization, and recovery is essential for compliance and resilience, and how non-linear cost behavior in agentic systems requires budget guardrails and outcome-based evaluation to deliver predictable ROI in production.

Title: Agent Evals That Check What Actually Happened
Abstract: A better answer score does not prove that an AI agent completed its task. Learn how to evaluate tool-using agents through observable actions and outcomes, and turn those checks into release decisions for code, prompt and model changes.  An agent can produce a convincing completion message while a tool request remains unresolved, an action has been repeated, or a required approval was missing. A text-only evaluation can reward the response while overlooking the execution failure. Conversely, an agent that refuses every action is not a reliable system simply because it avoids unsafe effects.  Drawing on Sajal Garg's work on automated LLM evaluation infrastructure at Microsoft AI, this session develops an evaluation workflow around a non-confidential illustrative task. It separates deterministic checks on actions and service state from quality judgments on generated content, distinguishes infrastructure and judge failures from task failures, and uses controlled interruption and lost-acknowledgement cases to test recovery. It also explains why test state must be reset and variable behavior evaluated across repeated runs.  The closing section connects the results to regression gates: compare current and candidate versions on the same cases, preserve the versioned inputs and checks, and keep critical execution failures separate from aggregate quality scores. Attendees leave with a failure taxonomy, concrete action/effect assertions and a practical agent-evaluation release checklist. This is an operational evaluation session, not a worker-pool architecture talk or product demonstration.

Title: Building a KPI-Agnostic Anomaly Detection Pipeline for Retail Operations at Scale
Abstract: Most anomaly detection systems are built for a single metric and have to be rebuilt every time the business asks a new question. This talk walks through the design of a generalizable, KPI-agnostic anomaly detection pipeline built for a retail network of roughly 3,000 stores, starting with foot traffic data and designed to extend to any time-series KPI with minimal changes. It covers why a three-model ensemble (Prophet, Isolation Forest, and an autoencoder) outperformed any single approach, how severity scoring and automated reason-labeling were layered on top, and the practical data quality problems that showed up along the way, from zero-traffic days to extreme outliers. The talk closes with the roadmap for adding LLM-based root cause reasoning to explain anomalies automatically.

Title: From PoC to Production: Deploying Agentic AI at Enterprise Scale
Abstract: Most agentic AI demos never survive contact with production. Brittle prompts, no evaluation harness, no guardrails, no ownership model, and the prototype quietly dies after the demo. This case study walks through taking an agentic AI system from prototype to a production deployment serving merchants across more than 600 retail locations. It covers the architecture (multi-agent orchestration for assortment planning and optimization), the evaluation and data-contract testing that run in CI, the default-deny data governance layer, monitoring and cost/latency tradeoffs in production, and the failure modes that only appear at scale. Attendees leave with a concrete checklist for moving their own agent prototypes into production: what to instrument first, which gates actually caught bugs, and the organizational changes (ownership, on-call, stakeholder trust) that mattered as much as the technology.

JobTitle1: Making Security Risk Intelligence Mainstream ,AI Exchange Author
Title: Automating the 'Governance': Building a Rules Engine for AI Use Case Governance at Scale
Abstract: Every enterprise deploying AI faces the same problem: hundreds of teams want to ship AI features, and security needs to evaluate each one. Manual review doesn't scale. Spreadsheet-based tracking breaks. And without clear automated rules, governance becomes either a rubber stamp or a permanent bottleneck.     This session presents a practical rules engine architecture for AI use case governance that evaluates deployment requests against policy rules defined in YAML, with short-circuit 'red zone' logic for automatic rejection of high-risk patterns and graduated approval workflows for everything else. The engine processes JSON context from intake forms, evaluates against tiered policy rules, and produces auditable approval or rejection decisions.     The talk covers the full system: rule definition, evaluation logic, red zone short-circuiting, general approval criteria, integration with existing GRC workflows, and lessons learned from operating the system across dozens of AI use case submissions.     Key Learnings  • Why manual AI use case governance fails at enterprise scale and what to automate first  • Designing a rules engine with YAML-defined policies and JSON context evaluation  • Red zone short-circuit logic: automatically rejecting high-risk AI patterns without human review  • Graduated approval workflows: tiered governance based on risk classification  • Integrating automated governance into existing security review and GRC workflows

Title: Testing Agents for Permission Leaks: Authorization Evals in the Delivery Pipeline
Abstract: Most agent evaluation suites measure accuracy, helpfulness, and task completion. Few test whether the agent reveals data the current user isn’t allowed to see. In regulated environments, that gap is the one that matters most.  This talk shows how to treat authorization as a testable property of an agent system and run it in the delivery pipeline like any other regression suite. Drawing on experience building multi-agent systems over enterprise banking CRM data, it covers:  Persona-based test users with different entitlements running the same tasks Leak assertions that check responses, summaries, and tool calls for restricted facts Combination tests that catch disclosures created when individually permitted results are joined Regression triggers for model upgrades, prompt changes, and new tools Making failures debuggable by linking each leak to the tool call and context that caused it  Attendees will leave with a blueprint for adding authorization evals to their agent release process.

Title: Edge MLOps: Building a Pipeline from PyTorch Training to On-Device Inference with ExecuTorch
Abstract: Most MLOps pipelines end at a cloud endpoint. When the target is a phone, the pipeline has to account for memory limits, thermal budgets, battery drain, and a fleet of devices with very different hardware. Drawing on contributions to Meta's open-source PyTorch ExecuTorch runtime, this talk walks through what an edge-focused MLOps pipeline needs:  Exporting PyTorch models into a mobile runtime built on a model loader, execution planner, memory manager, and operator registry Making compression part of the pipeline: quantization-aware training, structured pruning, and knowledge distillation Why quantization-aware training preserves accuracy better than post-training quantization alone Validating models across device tiers, including NPU versus CPU execution paths Fitting models within binary-size and thermal constraints before release  Attendees leave with a reference pipeline for taking models from training to production on consumer mobile devices.

Title: Shared Control Planes for Generative AI and ML Platforms
Abstract: As Generative AI adoption grows, many enterprises add separate AI infrastructure beside existing machine learning platforms, creating duplicated governance, observability, lineage, model registries, deployment pipelines, and operating processes. This session presents a practical MLOps integration pattern for extending existing ML platforms to support both predictive AI and Generative AI through a shared control plane while keeping workload-specific runtime optimization.  Attendees will learn how classical ML and Generative AI workloads can run across online, near-real-time, and batch serving environments without a full platform redesign. The session explains how common capabilities such as model registry, lineage, observability, identity, governance, rollout strategies, and cost attribution can be reused across both workload types, while runtime extensions support LLM serving, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, token streaming, continuous batching, multi-node inference, and unified evaluation workflows.  The session also covers Kubernetes-based reference architecture patterns, deployment contracts, promotion gates, policy enforcement, security controls, operational governance, and cost management practices that help teams absorb Generative AI into existing ML ecosystems with less duplication. Attendees will leave with practical guidance for balancing scalability, safety, observability, performance, and operational efficiency while modernizing enterprise AI platforms under a unified MLOps foundation.

Title: When Bad Data Reaches the Model: Engineering Data Quality Into MLOps at Healthcare Scale
Abstract: Every machine learning system depends on the data feeding it, and in healthcare that data arrives messy, incomplete, and in enormous volume. A single mismatched record can send the wrong information to the wrong patient, so data quality is not a convenience. It is a safety requirement.  In this session I will walk through how my team built real time, cloud native pipelines that treat data quality, validation, and anomaly detection as core parts of the MLOps lifecycle rather than a cleanup step at the end. I will show the design choices that let these pipelines process millions of events a day without falling over, the checks that catch bad records before they ever reach a model, and the ways we measure quality once a system is running in production.  I will also be honest about the parts that did not go smoothly, the assumptions that broke under real load, and what I would build differently today. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for making data quality a central part of their own pipelines, whether they work in healthcare or any field where trust in the data matters.

JobTitle1: National Institute of Technology, Jamshedpur, India
Title: Engineering Cloud Infrastructure for Agentic AI: MLOps and Self-Healing Systems
Abstract: Agentic AI is reshaping how cloud infrastructure is designed, deployed, and operated. As autonomous systems increasingly perceive, reason, and act, traditional cloud architectures face challenges in managing unpredictable workloads, low-latency requirements, and dynamic resource demands. This session explores practical architectural approaches to building scalable, reliable, and adaptive infrastructure for agentic AI through MLOps principles.  The talk examines how Kubernetes, multi-cloud environments, and orchestration frameworks such as LangChain can support agentic AI workloads. It highlights architectural considerations for resource scaling, workload orchestration, infrastructure automation, and operational efficiency.  A key focus is self-healing cloud operations, where collaborative AI agents can assist with incident detection, automated remediation, and system recovery. The session also explores observability and automation maturity gaps that affect reliability, performance, and service-level objectives.  Attendees will gain insights into designing agentic AI infrastructure with security, governance, compliance, and cost optimization in mind, along with practical considerations for integrating autonomous operations into existing cloud environments.

Title: MLOps for AI-Driven Municipal Bond Intelligence and Execution
Abstract: Municipal bonds finance essential U.S. infrastructure, but their lifecycle produces large volumes of documents, disclosures, financial data, market information, and trading inputs across municipalities, advisors, underwriters, investors, and trading desks. This session presents a practical architecture for applying MLOps principles to connect these information flows and continuously operate AI-driven municipal bond intelligence.  The workflow begins with an AI Document Intelligence Assistant that processes official statements, financial reports, continuing disclosures, ratings, and security information from sources such as EMMA/MSRB and Bloomberg. It extracts attributes including CUSIP, coupon, maturity, call provisions, revenues, outstanding debt, debt-service coverage, pension obligations, and covenants. Validation against prior filings and reference data supports credit and anomaly detection for identifying material changes, disclosure inconsistencies, financial deterioration, or improving credit conditions.  The resulting intelligence feeds a Portfolio Manager AI Assistant that evaluates credit quality alongside yield curves, relative value, duration, liquidity, ratings, portfolio exposure, investment guidelines, and state and sector concentration. The system presents Buy, Hold, Sell, or Review recommendations while keeping the portfolio manager as the final decision-maker.  After approval, a Trader AI Assistant evaluates fair value and liquidity, supports dealer and RFQ strategy, analyzes quotes, and helps document explainable best-execution decisions. The architecture then extends into a six-stage operational feedback loop: Document AI → Credit Intelligence → Portfolio Manager AI → Trader AI → Post-Trade AI → Continuous Monitoring.  The session focuses on practical architecture, automation, validation, monitoring, explainability, and continuous feedback, showing how MLOps practices can help operate AI workflows reliably across the municipal bond lifecycle.

Title: Scaling Microservices Observability with Agentic LLMs
Abstract: Modern microservices generate massive volumes of logs, metrics, and distributed traces, making incident detection, root cause analysis, and service reliability increasingly challenging. Traditional observability tools often struggle to correlate signals across complex service dependencies, resulting in delayed investigations and operational blind spots.  This session explores how Agentic Large Language Models (LLMs) can enhance cloud-native observability through semantic analysis, intelligent telemetry correlation, automated causal reasoning, and closed-loop remediation.  Focusing on architecture and operational practices, the presentation examines approaches to integrating LLM-driven analysis into existing observability workflows. Drawing on published research and industry findings, it discusses improvements in event correlation, service dependency mapping, alert accuracy, and incident response, including reductions in Mean Time to Detection (MTTD) and Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR).  Attendees will gain insights into scalability, performance optimization, debugging, security, data privacy, and governance considerations. The session highlights practical approaches to improving observability, automating incident response, and maintaining resilient distributed systems at scale.

Title: Hardening LLM Inference Containers: Risk-Based Vulnerability Management in MLOps
Abstract: Deploying large language models in production requires secure, reliable container images, yet complex dependency trees often generate thousands of vulnerability findings that delay releases and overwhelm MLOps teams. This session presents a practical case study on reducing container security risks by distinguishing vulnerability counts from actual exploitable exposure. Using a production LLM inference image, we examine how operating system packages accounted for approximately 93% of reported vulnerabilities but contributed relatively few critical or high-severity findings. Conversely, Python dependencies represented only 6% of findings while accounting for nearly two-thirds of severe vulnerabilities. Unused multimedia libraries further inflated scanner reports without contributing to inference functionality. The talk demonstrates an actionable MLOps hardening workflow combining minimal base images, multi-stage Docker builds, dependency analysis, and targeted Python package remediation. We explore how identifying unnecessary packages, vendored dependencies, and redundant manifests can reduce security noise while preserving inference functionality and deployment reliability. Through this approach, vulnerability findings decreased from over 4,000 to fewer than 40, with zero critical or high-severity findings within three weeks. Attendees will learn practical techniques for integrating risk-based vulnerability assessment into CI/CD pipelines, improving container maintainability, and accelerating secure LLM deployment without compromising operational performance.

Title: Building Resilient MLOps Pipelines for Illiquid Loan Portfolio Valuation
Abstract: Financial institutions rely on complex models to value mortgages, commercial loans, and other illiquid lending assets under changing market conditions. Moving these models into reliable production environments requires more than accurate calculations—it requires scalable pipelines, reproducibility, observability, and strong controls around data and model changes.  This session presents a practical MLOps architecture for building and operating resilient loan portfolio valuation systems. It explores how market data ingestion, configurable economic scenarios, prepayment assumptions, cash-flow models, and discounting workflows can be organized into repeatable valuation pipelines. The session examines versioning of data, model configurations, and assumptions so teams can reproduce historical valuations, investigate unexpected results, and safely introduce model updates.  The session also covers operational considerations including automated testing, pipeline monitoring, data lineage, failure handling, model validation, and auditability. Event-driven processing patterns are explored as a way to respond efficiently to changes in market data and portfolio positions while supporting scalable computation. Attendees will learn practical architectural principles for transforming financial valuation models into maintainable production systems where reliability, traceability, and reproducibility are treated as core MLOps requirements.

Title: Green Evals, Broken Agents: Making Evals a First-Class Deployment Artifact
Abstract: An agent's eval suite can be green while the agent is broken. Dylan Ler has run evals and deployment as a practitioner and kept hitting the same failures in his own published experiments. In his Latent Pager Memory study, reporting only F1 and latency made the method look like a clean win (+41.5% F1, 2.55x faster); adding hallucination (0.292 to 0.580) turned that win into a design problem. Selecting checkpoints by validation loss instead of the metric that mattered would have cost about 35% F1. A one-line generation fix moved test F1 more than any architecture change. In his calibration audit, accuracy and Brier score ranked models in opposite orders. In 'Worlds That Teach Back', 85.6% token accuracy said nothing about whether generated physics conserved energy.  The talk turns those lessons into a pipeline: datasets, graders, and thresholds versioned and owned; deterministic checks alongside calibrated LLM judges; evals that score trajectories, invariants, and tool calls, not only final answers; a sentinel suite on every prompt, tool, or model change; and every observed failure turned into a minimal regression test with a measured reproduction rate. Attendees leave with a CI blueprint and a budget for what to run per PR, nightly, and pre-release.

Title: Build ML Workflows with Codex, Flyte, and MCP
Abstract: AI coding tools can write ML code, but reliable execution still needs orchestration. This talk shows how to connect Codex to Flyte through MCP for a reproducible training or evaluation workflow.  I will talk about how OpenAI hosts Flyte for internal training, and how we developed MCP for integration with Codex.  Attendees will leave with a practical workflow pattern and a checklist for debugging, reproducibility, and safe execution.

Title: Agents That Check Their Own Work: The Validator Pattern
Abstract: An analytics agent that is right most of the time still can't be trusted with business questions, because nobody knows which answers are the wrong ones. This talk covers a simple pattern that changes that. Specialist agents can only read data, and a separate validator checks every claim in a draft answer against its live source before the answer goes out. We'll look at how to split the work between specialists and validator, what the validator should check and what it shouldn't, and how to handle answers it rejects. We'll also cover the failures that showed up in practice, including outages nobody noticed at first, and the operating rules that came out of them.
